analysis.one_liner: Restores the FTC's power to sue companies that defraud consumers and win their money back.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced July 30, 2026, with 2 cosponsors, referred to two House committees, and has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: After a 2021 Supreme Court ruling (AMG Capital Management v. FTC), the Federal Trade Commission could no longer use one of its main enforcement tools to win refunds for consumers cheated by scams and deceptive practices. This bill amends the FTC Act to explicitly allow the FTC to seek permanent injunctions, restitution, refunds, contract rescission, and disgorgement of ill-gotten profits in federal court. It sets a 10-year lookback for such monetary relief. The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers who lose money to deceptive practices, scams, and fraud — debt relief schemes, bogus health products, pyramid-type offers — would have the FTC able to sue in court and win their money back, not just stop the conduct going forward. The FTC itself regains a lost enforcement tool; it had used this authority to recover billions for consumers before the 2021 ruling.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers cheated by scams and fraud

how_it_helps.text: Amends Section 13 of the FTC Act to let the FTC seek permanent injunctions and 'such other relief as the court determines to be just and proper,' in addition to the temporary bans it already had [S2].

Creates an explicit equitable-relief power: courts may order restitution for losses, rescission or reformation of contracts, refunds, return of property, and disgorgement of any unjust enrichment a violator obtained from the violation [S2].
The relief can reach conduct going back 10 years before the FTC files suit, with time out of the U.S. not counted toward the limit [S2].
The new authority applies to actions pending on, or started after, the date of enactment [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that engage in deceptive practices would have to return money they obtained — paying restitution and disgorging profits in FTC enforcement suits. Businesses generally face expanded enforcement exposure, including a 10-year lookback and application to pending cases. Some enforcement and litigation costs could be passed to consumers in prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill expands the FTC's enforcement power significantly, including a 10-year lookback and retroactive application to cases already pending, which businesses argue creates uncertainty and liability for conduct long past [S2].

It defines monetary relief primarily as returning gains and making victims whole (disgorgement is offset by restitution paid), limiting punitive recovery, but judgments can still be large and legal fights costly, and any costs may ultimately be spread across a company's customers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill restores consumer compensation for fraud victims that courts took away in 2021; the main costs fall on companies found to have violated FTC-enforced law, plus higher legal uncertainty for legitimate businesses given the long lookback. On balance the consumer benefit is direct and the cost falls mostly on firms that engaged in the deceptive conduct.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two House committees in July 2026, and neither committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky (D-IL) introduced the bill on July 30, 2026, joined by Reps. Yvette Clarke (D-NY) and Robert Menendez (D-NJ) [S1] [S2].
The Speaker referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, the Judiciary Committee, so each would handle provisions in its jurisdiction [S4].
Two House Democrats cosponsored the bill [S3].
No committee action, floor action, or vote has occurred since referral, and the current Congress ends January 3, 2027 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that might have faced FTC suits seeking restitution and disgorgement are better off because the bill has not advanced; consumers defrauded by deceptive practices remain without the FTC's pre-2021 money-recovery tool.

for.name: Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore the FTC's authority to seek refunds and disgorgement in court.

for.name: Yvette Clarke and Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; all three named members are Democrats and no opposition has been recorded on the bill itself.

industries.industry: Companies that engage in deceptive practices (telemarketers, debt relief and health product schemes, pyramid-type sellers)
industries.note: The bill would let the FTC claw back profits and win refunds for their victims, restoring the FTC's main monetary remedy lost in the 2021 AMG Capital ruling. Before that ruling the FTC had used it to return billions to consumers [S2].
They could face costly FTC suits and a 10-year lookback even when conduct was long past or claims are contested. Some cost may be passed to consumers in prices.
The agency regains a tool for obtaining refunds and disgorgement in federal court that courts stripped in 2021 [S2].

analysis.trajectory: Introduced with only 2 cosponsors, referred to two committees, and with no markup or hearing as the Congress nears its January 3, 2027 end, the bill is very unlikely to advance; versions of this fix introduced in prior Congresses have also died in committee.
